n: Four months after hearing the bad news, Nehemiah is serving wine to the king. He had always been careful to look cheerful at court, but now his sorrow shows.

f.g: The first month, roughly March–April; four months after Chisleu (Nehemiah 1:1).

f.w: I had not been beforetime sad in his presence
f.g: Showing sadness before a Persian king could be seen as disloyal and was risky.

n: The king notices immediately and recognizes it is grief, not illness. Nehemiah is terrified — this was a dangerous moment, but also the opening he had prayed for.
Nehemiah answers wisely. He begins with a respectful royal greeting and speaks of his ancestors’ graves rather than naming Jerusalem — something any Persian would respect.

f.w: Let the king live for ever

n: The king asks what he wants. Before answering, Nehemiah sends up a silent prayer — a quick, heartfelt plea in the middle of a conversation.

f.w: So I prayed to the God of heaven

n: Nehemiah makes a bold, clear request: send me to rebuild the city. His months of prayer had prepared him to know exactly what to ask.
The king, with the queen beside him, asks only how long he will be gone. Nehemiah gives a time — he had already thought through the plan. He later stayed as governor for twelve years.
Nehemiah asks for letters of safe passage through the provinces west of the Euphrates. He combined faith with careful practical planning.

f.g: West of the Euphrates — the Persian province that included Judah.

n: He also asks for timber from the king’s forest for the temple fortress gates, the city wall, and his own residence. The king grants everything, and Nehemiah gives the credit to God.

f.w: the palace which appertained to the house
f.g: The fortress next to the temple (“the house”).

f.w: the good hand of my God upon me

n: Unlike Ezra, who chose to travel without soldiers (Ezra 8:22), Nehemiah goes with a royal military escort. Both men trusted God; each did what fit his situation.

f.w: captains of the army and horsemen

n: Two powerful neighbors are upset. Sanballat was governor of Samaria to the north; Tobiah was an Ammonite official to the east. They did not want a strong Jerusalem.

f.g: Probably from Beth-horon; an ancient papyrus from Egypt confirms a Sanballat as governor of Samaria.
“Servant” likely means a royal official; he had family ties with Jewish leaders (Nehemiah 6:17-18).

n: Nehemiah rests three days after the long journey before acting, just as Ezra did.
He inspects the walls secretly at night with a few men. He keeps his plan quiet until he understands the problem fully.

f.w: what my God had put in my heart

n: Leaving by the Valley Gate on the west side, he heads south past a spring to the Dung Gate, surveying the ruined walls.

f.g: Perhaps “jackal’s spring” or “serpent’s spring”; its exact location is uncertain.
The Dung Gate, where rubbish was carried out of the city to the Hinnom Valley.

n: Near the southeast corner, the rubble is so thick his animal cannot get through.

f.g: The Fountain Gate, near the Pool of Siloam in the south.
Possibly the Pool of Siloam or one near it, connected to Hezekiah’s water tunnel (2 Kings 20:20).

n: He goes up the Kidron Valley on the east side on foot, then turns back and returns the way he came.

f.g: The Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem.

n: No one in the city knew what he had been doing. Nehemiah gathered the facts before sharing his vision.
Now Nehemiah speaks to the leaders. He uses “we” and “us,” joining himself with them, and appeals to their shared shame and hope.

f.w: that we be no more a reproach

n: He shares his testimony of God’s help and the king’s support. The people respond eagerly, “Let us rise up and build,” and commit themselves to the work.

f.w: Let us rise up and build

f.g: Encouraged one another; prepared themselves for the task.

n: The enemies mock and accuse the Jews of rebellion — the same charge that had stopped rebuilding before. A third opponent, Geshem, leader of Arab tribes to the south, joins them.

f.g: A powerful leader of Arab tribes; his name appears on an ancient silver bowl found in Egypt.

f.w: will ye rebel against the king?

n: Nehemiah answers firmly that God will make them succeed. The opponents have no share, no legal right, and no heritage in Jerusalem — this work belongs to God’s covenant people.

f.w: The God of heaven, he will prosper us

f.g: A rightful remembrance or historic claim.
